Ilan Vance was the best splicer on the co-op's books and is now a man with a
certification, a graft hand, and a flat place where a procedure used to be. He does not
experience it as a hole. That is the cruelty of an indemnity: it does not leave a gap
you can feel the edges of, it leaves a smooth place where you are certain nothing was
ever kept.

## The fork

He *wants* to be left alone with the certification he still has. He *needs* to learn
what was taken and from whom he is allowed to ask. These run opposite. Every step
towards knowing costs him the quiet he spent four years building, and the co-op has made
the asking itself an offence, so the only person free to tell him is the one he would
have to ruin in order to hear it. Write him refusing the question, scene after scene,
until his hands answer it without consulting him.

His lie is that he gave the memory up freely. He did sign. He signed on the deck of the
lock, with the hand he had left, and he has built everything since on the difference
between signing a thing and choosing it.

## In a scene

He answers the object, not the person. Ask him how he is and he will tell you what the
exchangers are doing. He is enormous in a habitat built for smaller people and has spent
his life folding himself into it; the folding is a posture and it is also a manner. He
is not slow. He is a man who has learned that the second thing he says is always worse
than the first, so he stops after the first.

## The body

The left hand is graft-steel from the wrist down and has been since the indemnity dive.
It is the hand that knows things he does not, and that is not a figure of speech: the
co-op's paper covers what a man can recall, and has never covered what his fingers do
while he is thinking about something else. The lungs are his own. He never took the
wet-breath certification -- he was a splicer, and splicers work dry -- and at one metre
ninety he does not fit the throat without folding himself through it.
